claim: Traditional herbal medicines provide an exciting starting point for discovery of new immunomodulatory drugs.
source: Traditional herbal medicines, which emphasize a holistic, patient-centric view of disease treatment, provide an exciting starting point for discovery of new immunomodulatory drugs.
evidence: This is a stated position in the abstract without specific supporting data or citations in this sentence.

claim: Progress on identification of herbal molecules with proven single agent activity has been slow.
source: Progress on identification of herbal molecules with proven single agent activity has been slow, in part because of insufficient consideration of pharmacology fundamentals.
evidence: This is an assessment of the field's progress without specific data or citations provided.

claim: Many molecules derived from medicinal plants exhibit low oral bioavailability and rapid clearance.
source: Many molecules derived from medicinal plants exhibit low oral bioavailability and rapid clearance, leading to low systemic exposure.
evidence: This is stated as a general observation about plant-derived molecules, drawing on established pharmacological knowledge.

claim: Plant-derived molecules with low oral bioavailability can act locally in the gut or liver to activate xenobiotic defense pathways that trigger beneficial systemic effects on the immune system.
source: Recent research suggests that such molecules can act locally in the gut or liver to activate xenobiotic defense pathways that trigger beneficial systemic effects on the immune system.
evidence: This is presented as a hypothesis based on recent research, though specific citations are not provided in this sentence.

claim: Small molecules offer important benefits over biologic drugs, including easier manufacturing and greater affordability once off patent.
source: However, small molecules still offer important benefits. Notably, they are much easier to manufacture and more affordable once they come off patent, which suits global needs.
evidence: This is based on general knowledge about pharmaceutical manufacturing and economics.

claim: Kinase inhibitors of JAK, BTK, and SYK have been approved to downregulate specific immune pathways in various diseases.
source: One small-molecule class, kinase inhibitors, has been extensively explored for immunomodulation, and inhibitors of JAK, BTK, and SYK kinases have been approved to downregulate specific immune pathways in various diseases (Zarrin et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zarrin et al., 2021.

claim: There is great interest in adding small molecules in combination to help patient subgroups that are insufficiently responsive to single biologics.
source: There is also great interest in adding small molecules in combination to help patient subgroups that are insufficiently responsive to single biologics (Adams et al., 2015; van der Zanden et al., 2020; Ahmed et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Combining ingredients with complementary actions is central to the TCM philosophy.
source: Combining ingredients with complementary actions is central to the TCM philosophy (Zhang et al., 2014), which prompted the application of systems pharmacology approaches to rationally decipher existing combinations and develop new ones (Li et al., 2012; Ru et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2014.

claim: Systems pharmacology approaches have been applied to rationally decipher existing TCM combinations and develop new ones.
source: Combining ingredients with complementary actions is central to the TCM philosophy (Zhang et al., 2014), which prompted the application of systems pharmacology approaches to rationally decipher existing combinations and develop new ones (Li et al., 2012; Ru et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Li et al., 2012 and Ru et al., 2014.

claim: Physical emulsions naturally present in herbal extracts may increase oral bioavailability of active components compared to pure molecules.
source: The physical emulsions naturally present in herbal extracts may also increase oral bioavailability of active components compared to pure molecules (Zhao et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zhao et al., 2020.

claim: Drug approval in the West usually requires a pure molecule with a precisely defined formulation to demonstrate single agent activity before combinations can be tested.
source: However, drug approval in the West usually requires a pure molecule with a precisely defined formulation to demonstrate single agent activity before combinations can be tested, and we are convinced that many TCM molecules with useful single agent activity remain to be discovered.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of Western regulatory requirements for drug approval.

claim: Modulation of the gut microbiome by TCMs is an important research frontier.
source: Modulation of the gut microbiome by TCMs is an important research frontier (Lin et al., 2019b; Lin et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2020a; Li et al., 2021b).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Traditional TCM prescriptions mainly consist of dried plant and fungal ingredients boiled in water and administered as oral decoctions.
source: Traditional TCM prescriptions mainly consist of dried plant and fungal ingredients boiled in water and administered as oral decoctions.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about traditional TCM preparation methods.

claim: Western drugs designed for oral dosing are usually optimized to maximize adsorption through the gut wall and minimize metabolism by the liver.
source: Western drugs designed for oral dosing are usually optimized using synthetic chemistry and formulation methodology to maximize adsorption through the gut wall and minimize metabolism by the liver.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of Western pharmaceutical drug development.

claim: Some famous plant-derived drugs display good pharmacology, such as morphine, digoxin, quinine and artemisinin.
source: Some famous plant-derived drugs display good pharmacology, such as morphine, digoxin, quinine and artemisinin.
evidence: This is based on established pharmacological knowledge about these well-known drugs.

claim: Most TCM molecules display poor pharmacology, including poor oral bioavailability, short plasma half-life and rapid metabolism by the gut and liver.
source: However, most TCM molecules display 'poor pharmacology', that is poor oral bioavailability, short plasma half-life and rapid metabolism by the gut and liver (Lin et al., 2019b; Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lin et al., 2019b and Chen et al., 2016.

claim: The gut microbiome may play a role in mediating systemic actions of some oral TCM components that are poorly absorbed.
source: The gut microbiome may play a role in mediating systemic actions of some oral TCM components that are poorly absorbed (Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2016.

claim: Plants and fungi evolved complex, bioactive metabolites mainly to deter herbivores through bitter taste or/and poisonous actions.
source: Plants and fungi evolved complex, bioactive metabolites, which we will term "xenobiotics", mainly to deter herbivores through bitter taste or/and poisonous actions.
evidence: This is based on established evolutionary biology knowledge.

claim: Animals evolved xenobiotic defenses to protect them from potential toxins in their diets.
source: In parallel, animals evolved xenobiotic defenses to protect them from potential toxins in their diets (Florsheim et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Florsheim et al., 2021.

claim: Animals that could safely digest toxic plants gained a competitive advantage in access to food resources.
source: Animals that could safely digest toxic plants gained a competitive advantage in access to food resources.
evidence: This is an inference based on evolutionary principles.

claim: The first layer of xenobiotic defenses in animals are sensory cues, such as bitter taste or bright colors, which signal avoidance of potentially poisonous foods.
source: The first layer of xenobiotic defenses in animals are sensory cues, such as bitter taste or bright colors, which signal avoidance of potentially poisonous foods.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of animal defense mechanisms.

claim: The gut wall is the most important barrier preventing systemic exposure to xenobiotics.
source: The second is a series of barriers that prevent systemic exposure, of which the gut wall is the most important.
evidence: This is based on established pharmacological knowledge.

claim: The liver efficiently removes many xenobiotics from the portal circulation before they enter the systemic circulation.
source: The liver efficiently removes many xenobiotics from the portal circulation before they enter the systemic circulation.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of liver function in drug metabolism.

claim: First pass metabolism by the liver is responsible for the poor pharmacology of many plant-derived xenobiotics that cross the gut barrier.
source: This filtering effect of the liver, which can be upregulated by prior exposure to xenobiotics, is called 'first pass metabolism' and is responsible for the poor pharmacology of many plant-derived xenobiotics that cross the gut barrier.
evidence: This is an inference based on established pharmacological principles.

claim: Xenobiotic defense systems of the gut, liver and kidney are dynamic and inducible.
source: Importantly, the xenobiotic defense systems of the gut, liver and kidney are dynamic. Maintaining high levels of defense is metabolically costly, therefore these systems evolved to be inducible.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of xenobiotic defense mechanisms.

claim: Exposure to xenobiotics induces defense proteins at the transcriptional level in the gut, liver and other organs.
source: Exposure to xenobiotics induces defense proteins, notably metabolic enzymes and transporters, at the transcriptional level in the gut, liver and other organs (Xie et al., 2004; Müller, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Xie et al., 2004 and Müller, 2000.

claim: Xenobiotics are detected in part by their toxic actions on cellular organelles and in part by dedicated receptor proteins.
source: Xenobiotics are detected in part by their toxic actions on cellular organelles and in part by dedicated receptor proteins which are thought to have evolved for xenobiotic sensing (Negishi et al., 2020; Hoffmann and Partridge, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Negishi et al., 2020 and Hoffmann and Partridge, 2015.

claim: PXR, FXR and AHR are examples of xenobiotic sensors that are prominent in hepatocytes.
source: Examples of xenobiotic sensors that are prominent in hepatocytes include the nuclear receptors PXR (Pregnane X receptor), FXR (Farnesoid X receptor) and AHR (Aryl Hydrocarbon Receptor).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of hepatocyte xenobiotic sensing.

claim: Nuclear receptors PXR, FXR and AHR bind xenobiotics through ligand-binding domains, leading to allosteric activation of their gene expression domains.
source: These receptors bind xenobiotics through the ligand-binding domains, leading to allosteric activation of their gene expression domains (Mackowiak and Wang, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mackowiak and Wang, 2016.

claim: KEAP1 detects oxidizing and alkylating xenobiotics using thiol chemistry.
source: The chaperone-like sensor KEAP1 (Kelch Like ECH Associated Protein 1) detects oxidizing and alkylating xenobiotics using thiol chemistry.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of KEAP1 function.

claim: Oxidation and alkylation of cysteines on KEAP1 cause it to be degraded, which releases and activates NRF2.
source: Oxidation and alkylation of cysteines on KEAP1 cause it to be degraded, which releases and activates its client protein, the transcription factor NRF2 (Baird and Yamamoto, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Baird and Yamamoto, 2020.

claim: NRF2 serves as a master activator of anti-oxidant and xenobiotic defenses.
source: NRF2 then serves as a master activator of anti-oxidant and xenobiotic defenses.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of NRF2 function.

claim: Activation of xenobiotic sensors in hepatocytes leads to induction of drug metabolizing enzymes, efflux pumps, anti-oxidant proteins and other defense factors.
source: Activation of xenobiotic sensors in hepatocytes leads to induction of drug metabolizing enzymes, such as cytochrome P450s, as well as efflux pumps, anti-oxidant proteins and other defense factors.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of hepatocyte xenobiotic responses.

claim: Induction of xenobiotic defenses, especially P450s, is an important cause of drug-drug interactions.
source: Induction of xenobiotic defenses, especially P450s, is an important cause of drug-drug interactions (Ma, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ma, 2008.

claim: Induction of xenobiotic defenses by drugs occurs in the liver, gut and other tissues.
source: Induction of xenobiotic defenses by drugs has been most studied in the liver, but it also occurs in the gut and other tissues (Dressman and Thelen, 2009; Stresser et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dressman and Thelen, 2009 and Stresser et al., 2021.

claim: The hepatocyte is the most important cell type for detecting and responding to xenobiotics.
source: The most important cell type for detecting and responding to xenobiotics is the hepatocyte.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of liver function in xenobiotic metabolism.

claim: Research on xenobiotic sensors has focused on regulation of drug metabolism and protection from cytopathic effects of toxins.
source: Research on xenobiotic sensors and the protective genes that they regulate has focused on two functions that are local to hepatocytes, that is, regulation of drug metabolism (Guengerich, 2017) and protection from the cytopathic effects of toxins, particularly by the KEAP1-NRF2 system (Taguchi and Kensler, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Guengerich, 2017 and Taguchi and Kensler, 2020.

claim: Activation of xenobiotic sensors in the gut or liver can induce secreted proteins whose effects extend to the whole body.
source: Of particular importance to this review is that activation of xenobiotic sensors in the gut or liver can induce secreted proteins, whose effects extend to the whole body.
evidence: This is an inference based on the authors' analysis of xenobiotic sensor function.

claim: Signaling proteins secreted by the gut or liver are termed enterokines and hepatokines, respectively.
source: Signaling proteins secreted by the gut or liver are termed, respectively, enterokines and hepatokines.
evidence: This is a definition based on established terminology.

claim: Many xenobiotics induce or repress hepatokines with known systemic actions, including IGF1, IGFALS, IGFBP, and GDF15.
source: A systematic analysis of drug- and toxin-induced changes in rat liver gene expression revealed that many xenobiotics induce or repress hepatokines with known systemic actions, including IGF1, IGFALS, IGFBP, and GDF15 (Shimada and Mitchison, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Shimada and Mitchison, 2019.

claim: Xenobiotic sensors in the liver can mobilize the whole human body to regulate feeding, metabolism and other physiological processes.
source: This regulation implies that xenobiotic sensors in the liver can mobilize the whole human body to regulate feeding, metabolism and other physiological processes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the regulation of hepatokines by xenobiotic sensors.

claim: Activation of xenobiotic defenses has been implicated in healthy aging of entire organisms.
source: Activation of xenobiotic defenses has been implicated in healthy aging of entire organisms (Hoffmann and Partridge, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hoffmann and Partridge, 2015.

claim: Xenobiotic sensors monitor gut microbiome metabolites.
source: Xenobiotic sensors also monitor gut microbiome metabolites (Stockinger et al., 2021), so they are a point of integration between direct- and microbiome-mediated effects of small molecules on the human body.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Stockinger et al., 2021.

claim: The innate immune system can detect and respond to xenobiotics.
source: The innate immune system can detect and respond to xenobiotics and we believe this system plays an important role in immunomodulation by herbal medicines, especially for molecules that lack oral bioavailability and act locally in the gut.
evidence: This is stated as a belief based on the authors' analysis, combining knowledge with speculation.

claim: Macrophages and dendritic cells in the lamina propria continuously sample the gut luminal contents by extending phagocytic processes directly into the gut lumen and by receiving material transcytosed by M cells.
source: Macrophages and dendritic cells in the lamina propria continuously sample the gut luminal contents by extending phagocytic processes directly into the gut lumen ('periscoping') and also by receiving material that is transcytosed out of the lumen by Microfold cells (M cells) (Bain and Schridde, 2018; Strober, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bain and Schridde, 2018 and Strober, 2009.

claim: Gut sampling by immune cells is important for monitoring the microbiome and triggering immune responses in the gut.
source: This sampling is important for monitoring the microbiome and triggering immune responses in the gut.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of gut immune function.

claim: Insoluble xenobiotics in particulate form can access the immune system through transcytosis and phagocytosis.
source: We propose it also constitutes a path by which insoluble xenobiotics that are unable to cross the gut wall due to their particulate form can access the immune system.
evidence: This is a proposal/hypothesis by the authors.

claim: Xenobiotic receptors in gut macrophages that have been implicated in sensing both microbiome metabolites and xenobiotics include AHR and TLRs.
source: Xenobiotic receptors in gut macrophages that have been implicated in sensing both microbiome metabolites and xenobiotics include AHR (Stockinger et al., 2021) and Toll-like receptors (TLRs) (Abreu, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Stockinger et al., 2021 and Abreu, 2010.

claim: TLRs can bind TCM polysaccharides.
source: TLRs are usually thought of as receptors for pathogen-derived molecules, but as we will discuss below, they can also bind TCM polysaccharides.
evidence: This is stated as a fact that will be discussed later in the manuscript.

claim: Modulation of gut macrophages and dendritic cells by luminal TCM molecules can modulate inflammation locally.
source: Modulation of gut macrophages and dendritic cells by luminal TCM molecules is expected to modulate inflammation locally, which may be important in treatment of gut inflammatory diseases, as discussed below.
evidence: This is an expectation/inference based on the authors' reasoning.

claim: Modulation of gut immune cells by TCM molecules can give rise to systemic effects by triggering secretion of circulating cytokines and by trafficking of educated leukocytes from the gut to other organs.
source: It can also give rise to systemic effects in at least two ways, by triggering secretion of circulating cytokines and by trafficking of educated leukocytes from the gut to other organs. We speculate both are important for relaying the effects of xenobiotic exposure from the gut to distant sites.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as speculation by the authors.

claim: Figure 1 illustrates models to explain how TCM molecules with poor pharmacology can act both locally and systemically.
source: Figure 1 illustrates a series of models to explain how TCM molecules with 'poor pharmacology' can act both locally and systemically.
evidence: This refers to Figure 1 which provides visual representation of the models.

claim: In recent years, TCM has evolved toward injectable formulations that bypass the gut barrier and achieve much higher plasma concentrations than oral dosing.
source: In recent years, TCM has evolved in the direction of injectable formulations that bypass the gut barrier and achieve plasma concentrations that are much higher than those achieved by traditional oral dosing (Li et al., 2018; Jiabo, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Li et al., 2018 and Jiabo, 2010.

claim: An injectable formulation of Panax ginseng extract can achieve plasma concentrations and systemic exposure values of ginsenosides that are many hundreds-fold higher than an oral decoction.
source: For example, an injectable formulation of Panax ginseng extract can achieve transient plasma concentrations and systemic exposure (AUC) values of the ginsenoside active ingredients that are many hundreds-fold higher than an oral decoction of the same herb, due to the poor oral bioavailability of ginsenosides (Choi et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2020b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Choi et al., 2020 and Zhang et al., 2020b.

claim: The safety of TCM prescriptions is mostly based on experience from traditional oral dosing, so it is important to critically evaluate potential toxicity when systemic exposure is drastically increased.
source: The safety of TCM prescriptions is mostly based on experience from traditional oral dosing so it is important to critically evaluate the potential for toxicity when systemic exposure is drastically increased (Li et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2019.

claim: Indigo naturalis is best known as a source of blue dye but also has traditional medicinal uses in China.
source: The plant Indigo naturalis is best known as a source of blue dye, but it also has traditional medicinal uses in China.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of Indigo naturalis.

claim: The main bioactive components of Indigo naturalis are the bis-indoles indigo and indirubin, which are formed by non-biological reactions during processing.
source: Its main bioactive components are the bis-indoles indigo and indirubin, which are formed by non-biological reactions during processing (Sun et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sun et al., 2021.

claim: Therapeutic benefit of Indigo naturalis in ulcerative colitis was proven by recent clinical trials.
source: Therapeutic benefit of Indigo naturalis in ulcerative colitis (UC, a common inflammatory disease of the colon) was proven by recent clinical trials (Naganuma et al., 2018; Naganuma et al., 2020; Uchiyama et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple clinical trials.

claim: Response rates for Indigo naturalis in ulcerative colitis were comparable to the most effective western drugs, including biologics that target TNFα.
source: Response rates for the herbal medicine were comparable to the most effective western drugs, including biologics that target TNFα, and patients whose disease was not well-managed by western drugs responded well to the herbal preparation (Naganuma et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Naganuma et al., 2020.

claim: Patients with ulcerative colitis whose disease was not well-managed by western drugs responded well to Indigo naturalis.
source: Response rates for the herbal medicine were comparable to the most effective western drugs, including biologics that target TNFα, and patients whose disease was not well-managed by western drugs responded well to the herbal preparation (Naganuma et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Naganuma et al., 2020.

claim: Indigo and indirubin are almost insoluble in water and have very poor oral bioavailability.
source: The active ingredients in Indigo Naturalis, Indigo and indirubin, are almost insoluble in water and have very poor oral bioavailability (Sun et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sun et al., 2021.

claim: Indigo and indirubin are thought to act directly in the gut where their concentration is locally high following ingestion of Indigo naturalis powder.
source: They are thought to act directly in the gut, where their concentration is locally high following ingestion of Indigo naturalis powder.
evidence: This is stated as a prevailing thought/hypothesis.

claim: Both indigo and indirubin are potent agonist ligands of AHR.
source: Both are potent agonist ligands of the prototypical xenobiotic sensor AHR (Adachi et al., 2001) and tests in knockout mice showed that AHR expression is required for the therapeutic activity of both Indigo naturalis and pure indigo (Kawai et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Adachi et al., 2001.

claim: AHR expression is required for the therapeutic activity of both Indigo naturalis and pure indigo.
source: Both are potent agonist ligands of the prototypical xenobiotic sensor AHR (Adachi et al., 2001) and tests in knockout mice showed that AHR expression is required for the therapeutic activity of both Indigo naturalis and pure indigo (Kawai et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kawai et al., 2017, describing knockout mouse experiments.

claim: Therapeutic action of indigo is thought to proceed via secretion of IL-10 and IL-22 from gut-associated immune cells.
source: Therapeutic action is thought to proceed via secretion of the protective cytokines IL-10 and IL-22 from gut-associated immune cells (Lin et al., 2019a; Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lin et al., 2019a and reference to Figure 2.

claim: Indigo particles are proposed to be delivered to gut macrophages and dendritic cells by phagocytosis, either directly from the gut lumen or following transcytosis by M cells.
source: We propose that indigo particles are delivered to gut macrophages and dendritic cells by phagocytosis, either directly from the gut lumen or following transcytosis by M cells (Bain and Schridde, 2018; Strober, 2009).
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a proposal by the authors, with citations supporting the mechanisms of phagocytosis and transcytosis.

claim: Once ingested by immune cells, active indigo molecule slowly leaches from the phagocytosed particle to activate AHR.
source: Once ingested, active molecule slowly leaches from the phagocytosed particle to activate AHR.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism by the authors.

claim: Limited clinical evidence suggests that the beneficial effects of Indigo naturalis powder can extend systemically.
source: Limited clinical evidence suggests that the beneficial effects of Indigo naturalis power can extend systemically (Sun et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sun et al., 2021.

claim: Systemic effects of Indigo naturalis may involve trafficking of indigo-loaded immune cells from the gut into the systemic immune system.
source: Rather, it may involve one of the indirect action pathways proposed in Figure 1, such as trafficking of indigo-loaded immune cells from the gut into the systemic immune system.
evidence: This is stated as a possibility/speculation by the authors.

claim: Systemic activation of AHR carries toxicity risk, as exemplified by TCDD-dioxin.
source: Systemic activation of AHR carries toxicity risk, as exemplified by the reference AHR agonist TCDD-dioxin (Bock and Köhle, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bock and Köhle, 2006.

claim: The gut-restricted distribution of indigo may be key to the therapeutic index of Indigo naturalis powder.
source: The gut-restricted distribution of the indigo molecule, which we propose is due to its insoluble nature and selective delivery to gut by transcytosis and phagocytosis of particles, may be key to the therapeutic index of Indigo naturalis power.
evidence: This is a proposal by the authors based on their reasoning.

claim: One proposed function of AHR in gut macrophages is to monitor the gut microbiome and its metabolites.
source: One of the proposed functions of AHR in gut macrophages is to monitor the gut microbiome and its metabolites (Stockinger et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Stockinger et al., 2021.

claim: The therapeutic action of indigo in ulcerative colitis can be viewed as restoring balance to an endogenous immuno-regulatory circuit that monitors the gut microbiome.
source: From this perspective, the therapeutic action of indigo in UC can be viewed as restoring balance to an endogenous immuno-regulatory circuit that monitors the gut microbiome.
evidence: This is an interpretation/perspective offered by the authors.

claim: Fungus-derived polysaccharides are perhaps the most widely studied TCM molecules with immunomodulatory activity.
source: Fungus-derived polysaccharides are perhaps the most widely studied TCM molecules with immunomodulatory activity.
evidence: This is an assessment based on the authors' knowledge of the field.

claim: Astragalus, Ganoderma, and Cordyceps are well-known examples of TCM herbs that stimulate the immune system, with polysaccharides believed to be one of their key active components.
source: Astragalus, Ganoderma, and Cordyceps are well-known examples of TCM herbs that stimulate the immune system and polysaccharides are believed to be one of their key active components.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in the TCM field.

claim: Lentinan was first approved in Japan for treating gastric cancer as a combinatorial agent with standard chemotherapies.
source: Lentinan, a polysaccharide derived from shiitake mushroom, was first approved in Japan for treating gastric cancer as a combinatorial agent with standard chemotherapies (Ina et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ina et al., 2013.

claim: Most clinical trial data for lentinan were from Japan and with relatively small patient cohorts.
source: Most of the clinical trial data so far were from Japan and with relatively small patient cohorts (Nakano et al., 1999; Oba et al., 2009; Ina et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple clinical trials.

claim: TCM-derived polysaccharides are used mainly as dietary supplements or adjuvant therapies.
source: Although evidence for immunomodulatory effects of TCM-derived polysaccharides is strong, their therapeutic effects in human are in general moderate and they are used mainly as dietary supplements or adjuvant therapies.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of current usage patterns.

claim: Available data suggest benefits of TCM-derived polysaccharides in prolonging survival and improving overall wellness of patients with advanced gastric cancer and liver cancer.
source: Available data suggest benefits in prolonging survival and improving the overall wellness of patients with advanced gastric cancer and liver cancer, but large trials with more diverse patient populations are needed to validate efficacy and extend usage.
evidence: This is an inference based on available data, though specific citations are not provided in this sentence.

claim: One well-documented immunomodulatory mechanism of TCM-derived polysaccharides is activation of Toll-like Receptors (TLRs) expressed on macrophages and dendritic cells.
source: One well-documented immunomodulatory mechanism of TCM-derived polysaccharides is activation of Toll-like Receptors (TLRs) that are expressed on macrophages and dendritic cells.
evidence: This is stated as well-documented, implying established knowledge.

claim: When activated by TCM-derived polysaccharides, TLRs upregulate cytokine signaling.
source: When activated by TCM-derived polysaccharides, they upregulate cytokine signaling.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of TLR function.

claim: Astragalus polysaccharides stimulate the TLR4 signaling pathway.
source: For example, Astragalus polysaccharides were shown to stimulate the TLR4 signaling pathway using a TLR4-defficient mouse model (Zhou et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zhou et al., 2017, describing experiments with TLR4-deficient mice.

claim: TLRs evolved to detect Pathogen Associated Molecular Patterns (PAMPs).
source: TLRs evolved to detect 'Pathogen Associated Molecular Patterns' (PAMPs).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of TLR evolution and function.

claim: Many PAMPs include sugar functionalities that are shared with plant- and fungus-derived TCM molecules.
source: Many PAMPs, such as components of bacterial and fungal cell walls, include sugar functionalities that are shared with plant- and fungus-derived TCM molecules, so it makes sense that fungus-derived polysaccharides are TLR activating ligands.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural similarities.

claim: The biological effects of TCM-derived polysaccharides are more subtle than classic TLR4 agonists such as E. coli lipopolysaccharide.
source: The biological effects of TCM-derived polysaccharides are more subtle than classic TLR4 agonists, such as E. coli lipopolysaccharide (LPS).
evidence: This is an observation based on comparing biological effects.

claim: Polysaccharides are probably most active within the gut lumen where they can interact with intestinal epithelial cells, gut microbiota, specialized immune cells and possibly chemoreceptors in the enteric nervous system.
source: Polysaccharides are probably most active within the gut lumen, where they can interact with the intestinal epithelial cells (IEC), the gut microbiota, specialized immune cells lining the gut and possibly also chemoreceptors in the enteric nervous system (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated as a probability/inference by the authors.

claim: The gut has developed intricate pattern recognition receptor (PRR) signaling cascades in multiple cell types to detect and distinguish different PAMPs through symbiotic co-evolution with commensal bacteria.
source: Through symbiotic co-evolution with commensal bacteria, the gut has developed intricate pattern recognition receptor (PRR) signaling cascades in multiple cell types to detect and distinguish different PAMPs so as to maintain homeostasis as well as trigger inflammatory responses (Bain and Schridde, 2018; Strober, 2009; Abreu, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bain and Schridde, 2018; Strober, 2009; and Abreu, 2010.

claim: Activation of intestinal PRR signaling by TCM-derived polysaccharides leads to production of pro-inflammatory cytokines and Interferons.
source: Similar to common PAMPs, activation of intestinal PRR signaling by TCM-derived polysaccharides and/or their metabolites produced by the gut microbes leads to the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines, such as IL-1β, IL-6, and IL-8, and Interferons (IFNα and IFNβ) (Fukata and Arditi, 2013; Kieser and Kagan, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fukata and Arditi, 2013 and Kieser and Kagan, 2017.

claim: Secondary inflammatory mediators from intestinal PRR activation generate systemic immunomodulatory effects upon secretion to the circulating blood.
source: These secondary inflammatory mediators then generate systemic immunomodulatory effects upon secretion to the circulating blood (Schirmer et al., 2016; Mainous et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Schirmer et al., 2016 and Mainous et al., 1995.

claim: Systemic drug effects may be mediated by drug-educated immune cells that traffic from the gut to distant sites.
source: Systemic drug effects may also be mediated by drug-educated immune cells that traffic from the gut to distant sites.
evidence: This is stated as a possibility by the authors.

claim: Intestinal T cells traffic to extra-intestinal lymph nodes and to the spleen.
source: For instance, intestinal T cells are known to traffic to extra-intestinal lymph nodes and to the spleen, and recent new data also revealed trafficking of intestinal γδ T cells to the brain that modulates the outcome of acute brain injury (Benakis et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge and a citation to Benakis et al., 2016 for the brain trafficking.

claim: Intestinal γδ T cells traffic to the brain and modulate the outcome of acute brain injury.
source: For instance, intestinal T cells are known to traffic to extra-intestinal lymph nodes and to the spleen, and recent new data also revealed trafficking of intestinal γδ T cells to the brain that modulates the outcome of acute brain injury (Benakis et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Benakis et al., 2016.

claim: Polysaccharide actions on the gut microbiota might cause changes in the gut and upregulate systemic immunomodulatory mediators.
